To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the leucophore, the white light scattering unit of the flexible skin in the cuttlefish Sepia officinalis, is composed of a large number of protein spheres that reflect light incoherently and that the leucosome microsphere is a unique, proteinaceous structure that is a candidate for bioinspired light scattering materials.
The cuttlefish leucosome, an ultrastructure of glycosylated, proteinacious microspheres, is the basis for a broadband, Lambertian white reflector.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
leucophores are an example of a simple, yet elegant, biophotonic structure that can be used as a model system to understand the physics of light scattering in complex biological systems.
the leucophore is a unique, biogenic, proteinaceous, white light reflector with a broadband, Lambertian scattering pattern that is not spectrally tuned to a particular wavelength.
the leucosome is a protein sphere that reflects white light and the leucophore is a cell that contains a large number of leucosomes and reflects white light.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a proteinaceous sphere with a refractive index of 1.51 can scatter white light.
the leucophore is the first example of a biophotonic structure in which the structural and compositional properties of the microspheres are tuned to produce white light scattering.
leucosomes in the leucophore are not spectrally or angle tuned, but instead are randomly ordered to produce broadband, Lambertian scattering.
